items.title: [popsci.com] Nearby giant likely tilted hot Jupiter out of view
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Astronomers say the hot Jupiter TOI-2535 b, about 1,000 light-years away, stopped transiting its star in March 2026 because the gravitational pull of a nearby, still-unseen planet tilted its orbit out of Earth’s line of sight. NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite observed the system from April 2019 to March 2026; the planet circles its star every 8.25 days. Before the transits vanished, they arrived as much as six hours early or late and grew shorter and shallower, signs that the orbit’s alignment was changing. How the planet moved close to its star remains uncertain. The study appeared in *The Astrophysical Journal Letters* on Nov. 9. TOI-2535 b is not expected to transit again for at least 30 years, while its companion could become visible in transit sooner.

items.title: [tuoitre.vn] European Hera probe begins examining asteroid struck in NASA deflection test
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft has begun surveying the Didymos asteroid pair from about 25 to 30 kilometers away, four years after NASA deliberately struck the smaller asteroid, Dimorphos, to test asteroid deflection. Hera’s first images show Didymos from a new angle, revealing boulders, craters and ridge-like features; some rocks may have been blasted from Dimorphos and traveled about 1 kilometer to the larger asteroid. The 2022 impact shortened Dimorphos’ orbit around Didymos by about 32 to 33 minutes and also altered the pair’s path around the sun. Hera’s close-up investigation aims to determine how the impact changed Dimorphos and why the deflection was greater than simulations predicted. The probe is expected to begin closer, more detailed observations next month, using 25 instruments and two CubeSats that will survey Dimorphos and attempt to land there.

items.title: [scientificamerican.com] Neanderthal DNA variant linked to smaller visual brain region, lower schizophrenia odds
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Researchers report that a Neanderthal-derived DNA variant is associated with a smaller occipital lobe and lower odds of schizophrenia in modern humans. In UK Biobank data, each copy of the variant corresponded to about 0.85 cubic centimeters less occipital-lobe volume; people with two copies had nearly 10% lower odds of schizophrenia than those with no copies. The occipital lobe processes visual information. The variant lies near DAAM1, a gene involved in brain development, but researchers have not established how it affects the brain or whether the smaller lobe explains the schizophrenia association. The variant was not associated with a meaningful difference in intelligence, and outside researchers cautioned against drawing conclusions about Neanderthal brain function from the findings in modern humans. The study was published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Its authors say further work, including studies using brain organoids or animal models, could investigate the mechanism.

Paleontologists have formally named *Vampyrocamelus welshi*, a long-legged camel that lived on the southern Great Plains about 13 million years ago. Fossils found mainly in Texas and Oklahoma indicate that it had a giraffe-like body and unusually large, backward-curving teeth that inspired its “vampire camel” nickname. Researchers identified the species from museum fossils, including skulls, jaws and limb bones, by comparing them with those of similar extinct camels. The formal description helps researchers recognize the animal in other fossil collections; the function of its teeth remains uncertain.

items.title: [theglobeandmail.com] North Atlantic right whale population falls to 382 as protections diverge
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

The North Atlantic right whale population fell to an estimated 382 animals at the end of 2025, down seven from the revised 2024 estimate, according to the North Atlantic Right Whale Consortium. The roughly 2% decline followed several years of slow growth. Scientists say the whales remain exposed to fishing-gear entanglements and vessel strikes as they migrate between Canadian and U.S. waters. The 2025-26 calving season produced 24 calves, the most since 2009. Researchers documented two whale deaths and eight human-caused injuries in 2026. Canada launched a whale-safe fishing gear strategy in February, while the U.S. House passed a bill to extend a pause on new protections for lobster and crab fisheries through 2035. The bill awaits Senate action.

items.title: [medicalxpress.com] Study links very large and small waists to higher death risk
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

A study of more than 17 million South Korean adults found that both unusually large and unusually small waist measurements were associated with a higher risk of death across weight and age groups. The lowest observed risk was associated with waist circumferences of 80–94 centimeters in men and 75–89 centimeters in women. The association between waist circumference and death risk was stronger at older ages, especially among women 75 and older. Researchers analyzed routine health-check measurements from 2009–10 and tracked survival for nearly 14 years, through June 30, 2024. The study was observational and cannot show that waist size causes death. Among people with normal weight or overweight whose waist circumference was high for their body mass index (BMI), reducing waist circumference without necessarily losing weight appeared to offer a greater survival benefit than losing weight while reducing waist circumference, the authors said.

items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

A draft COP31 agreement proposes at least $120 billion a year in adaptation finance for developing countries by 2035, alongside accelerated action to phase out fossil fuels. Released by the conference presidency on Nov. 16, the text remains under negotiation and does not represent an agreed position; the talks in Antalya, Türkiye, are scheduled to end Nov. 20. African negotiators are pressing for predictable grants, measurable delivery milestones and finance that does not deepen debt. The United Nations Environment Programme estimates developing countries will need $305 billion annually for adaptation by 2035, while international public adaptation finance reached $28.2 billion to $31.7 billion in 2024. Ghanaian Environment Minister Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings also called for funding to restore land and rivers damaged by mining and for greater local processing of Africa’s minerals.

items.title: [arstechnica.com] FAA plans to replace floppy-based air traffic systems by 2028
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

The Federal Aviation Administration plans to replace four aging information systems that rely on floppy disks with a unified digital platform at 435 air traffic facilities by the end of 2028. The new Enterprise Information Display System, or E-IDS, will consolidate weather alerts, airport status and flight notices that controllers currently retrieve through outdated, often manual processes. The FAA says the platform will give controllers faster access to safety-critical information and reduce maintenance problems. The agency has already upgraded five sites, while Congress has provided $12.5 billion for broader air traffic control modernization. The FAA is seeking additional funding through the proposed Modern Skies Act. The agency plans to deploy the system at the remaining locations by the end of 2028.

items.title: [theregister.com] Web-testing platform Optimizely breach exposes visitors at 178 sites to malware
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Hackers exploited a vulnerability in website-testing platform Optimizely on Nov. 16, injecting malicious JavaScript into scripts used by 178 organizations, including the BBC, CNN, Zoom, IKEA, HSBC and Salesforce. Security researcher Scott Helme and cybersecurity firm Report URI found that the code reached visitors through Optimizely’s trusted delivery infrastructure, without requiring attackers to break into each customer’s servers. The scripts attempted to replace cryptocurrency wallet addresses, capture card details entered into website forms, steal browser cookies, take screenshots and load exploit kits targeting older Apple iPhones and iPads. Report URI tracked about $7,040 in cryptocurrency sent to attacker-linked wallets in roughly nine hours. Researchers could not establish how many card details were stolen and reported no confirmed iPhone takeover in this campaign. Optimizely said it patched the flaw, removed the injected code, revoked tokens and reset access for affected accounts. Salesforce disabled the scripts while investigating, and IKEA opened an inquiry. Equifax stopped using the service and said it found no evidence its systems were compromised.
